title: Endpoints and the Extreme Value Theorem

steps.body:
On a **closed interval**, the biggest and smallest values are guaranteed to exist — and they can hide in only two places:

**at a critical point**, or **at an endpoint**.

That is the Extreme Value Theorem, and it turns optimisation into a finite checklist. Compute f at every critical point and at both ends; the largest wins.

explanationVariants: Critical point: f′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = 1 (in [0, 3]), where f(1) = −2. Endpoints: f(0) = 0 and f(3) = 18. The maximum is 18 — at an ENDPOINT, where the tangent is not flat at all.
A global maximum need not be a local one. On a closed interval the edges are always candidates.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 3]. Find the MAXIMUM value.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(1), the local MINIMUM at the critical point. The maximum is at the right endpoint: f(3) = 27 − 9 = 18.
That is f(0), the left endpoint. The right endpoint is far higher: f(3) = 18.
That is the endpoint's x-value. Its FUNCTION value is f(3) = 18.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Candidates: f(1) = −2, f(0) = 0, f(3) = 18. The maximum is 18, at an endpoint.

steps.body: Why the tangent need not be flat at the top.

widget.prompt: How a maximum can hide at an edge.

panels.title: Interior maxima are flat
panels.body: If the highest point is strictly INSIDE the interval, the curve must stop climbing and start falling — so f′ = 0 there. That is why critical points matter.

panels.title: Edges have no 'other side'
panels.body: At the right endpoint the curve may still be climbing hard. There is simply nowhere further to go. The tangent is steep, and the point is still the maximum.

panels.title: So check both
panels.body: The EVT does not say the maximum is at a critical point. It says it is at a critical point OR an endpoint — and the endpoint case is the one people forget.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the middle panel is the one that gets skipped.
widget.successFeedback: An interior maximum must be flat. An endpoint maximum need not be — it just runs out of room.

steps.body: The reveal's claim, live. Find the flat tangent yourself — then look at where the curve is actually tallest.

predict.prompt: This window shows f(x) = x³ on [−4, 4]. Somewhere the tangent goes flat. Will that flat point be the tallest point of the window?

options.label: No — the flat point isn't the top here
x³ never has a flat tangent

predict.reveal: Drag and watch the f′ pane: it touches zero at x = 0 while the curve climbs straight past — the tallest point is the right edge, where f′ = 48.

widget.prompt: Drag the point until the tangent is FLAT — drive f′ to zero — and watch what the curve does there.
widget.successFeedback: f′ = 0 at x = 0 — and yet the curve climbs straight past it. Flat found you a candidate, not the champion: the tallest point on this window is the right edge, where f′ = 48. That endpoint is exactly what the theorem makes you check.
widget.lowFeedback: Not flat yet — the f′ pane is still above zero here, and the curve is still climbing. Keep moving right toward where f′ dips to zero.
widget.highFeedback: You passed it — f′ is positive again and climbing. Back up to where the lower pane touches zero.

explanationVariants: The EVT needs a CONTINUOUS function on a CLOSED, bounded interval. Drop either condition and the guarantee vanishes.
On the open interval (0, 1), f(x) = x has no maximum: it approaches 1 without ever reaching it.

widget.prompt: Why does f(x) = x on the OPEN interval (0, 1) have no maximum?

options.label: It climbs all the way to 1 but never reaches it — the endpoint is not included.
options.feedback: Right, and that is precisely why the EVT insists on a CLOSED interval. Without the ends, the maximum can escape.

options.label: Because f′ is never zero.
options.feedback: True, but not the reason — on the CLOSED interval [0, 1] the same function has a maximum of 1, at an endpoint, with f′ still never zero.

options.label: Because it is not continuous.
options.feedback: f(x) = x is continuous everywhere. The failure is in the interval, not the function.

options.label: It does have one: 1.
options.feedback: 1 is not IN the open interval, so f never attains it. There is a supremum, but no maximum.

steps.body:
So the **closed-interval method** is a three-line recipe:

1. Find every critical point inside the interval.
2. Evaluate f there, and at both endpoints.
3. Pick the largest and the smallest.

No sign charts, no second derivatives. On a closed interval you simply compare a finite list of numbers.

explanationVariants: Critical points in [0, 3]: x = 1 only (x = −1 is outside). Plus the two endpoints. So three candidates.
Critical points OUTSIDE the interval are irrelevant and must be discarded.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 3]. How many candidates does the closed-interval method produce?

commonErrors.feedback: f′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1, but x = −1 is OUTSIDE [0, 3] and must be thrown away. That leaves x = 1 plus the two endpoints: three.
Do not forget the interior critical point x = 1. Two endpoints plus one critical point makes three.
The endpoints are candidates too — that is the whole point of the theorem.

widget.fallbackFeedback: x = 1 (inside), plus x = 0 and x = 3: three candidates.

hints: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = ±2. Which are inside [0, 3]?
Only x = 2. So the candidates are x = 0, x = 2 and x = 3.
explanationVariants: Candidates give 0, −16 and −9. The minimum is −16, at the critical point x = 2.
The maximum here is 0, at the LEFT endpoint — a reminder that both ends must be checked.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x on [0, 3]. Find the MINIMUM value.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(3), the right endpoint. The critical point x = 2 goes lower: f(2) = 8 − 24 = −16.
That is f(0), which is the MAXIMUM here. The minimum is −16.
That is where the minimum occurs. Its value is f(2) = −16.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Candidates: f(0) = 0, f(2) = −16, f(3) = −9. The minimum is −16.

takeaways: On a closed, bounded interval a continuous function ALWAYS attains a maximum and a minimum.
They hide only at critical points or at endpoints — an endpoint maximum need not have a flat tangent.
The closed-interval method is a finite checklist: evaluate, compare, done.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: the second derivative, and the shape of the bend.

concept.body: Make a list. Every critical point INSIDE the interval, plus both endpoints. Evaluate f at each. The biggest number on the list is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum. There is nowhere else to look.

explanationVariants: Candidates are f(0) = 1, f(2) = 5 and f(3) = 4, so the maximum is 5.
Compare all three; do not stop at the critical point.

widget.prompt: On [0, 3], f(0) = 1, f(3) = 4, and the only critical point gives f(2) = 5. What is the maximum?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the right endpoint. The critical point beats it: f(2) = 5.
That is WHERE the maximum occurs. Its value is 5.
